text.content:
Treasure and Rewards

A reward gives the heroes another choice. Coins can buy passage or supplies. A recipe can turn future ingredients into something useful. An introduction can open a door that no weapon would open safely. Choose rewards that make the next adventure more interesting and acknowledge what the company accomplished.

Use the @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.a8b099af3500d9f6.JournalEntryPage.cfa94361944ba875]{ordinary market} as the common price reference. HOL uses coins, with no metal denominations. Prices do not increase merely because a hero gains a level.

Begin with useful scale

A simple meal costs 1 coin and a plain bed costs 2 per night, meals separate. A Rope Coil costs 5; an ordinary melee weapon costs 12; a Lesser Healing Bottle costs 20. These anchors help you describe what a reward means to people in the world.

There is no established mandatory treasure total per level in this manuscript. Consider the party's current supplies, actual needs and opportunities to spend. A reward can be generous without buying a new discipline rank: coins purchase objects and services, while DP purchases character development.

RewardWhat the party gainsWhat it does not supply
CoinsFlexible purchasing power where goods are availableDP, discipline ranks or class signatures
EquipmentA specific physical objectUnprinted training or an extra attack
A supplyIts stated inventory die and usesGuaranteed charges equal to the die's faces
A recipeKnowledge of a particular productCrafting capability, tools or ingredients by itself
A serviceAn agreed attempt or period of workAutomatic Strong outcomes or unrestricted daily treatment
Information or accessA useful fact, route, introduction or permissionAuthority over everyone who hears of it

Put treasure where it belongs

Decide who owns an object and why it is there. A tool chest in a workshop, a road toll in a guard's pouch, and a carefully wrapped recipe in a cook's kit all tell something about their owners. The party can find useful goods without every creature carrying a purse calibrated to its CV.

Creature loot entries offer starting material. Adjust an individual's possessions to the scene before play: a bandit who has collected no tolls should not carry the same takings as one leaving a successful robbery. Keep the equipment required for its printed actions consistent with its description. Do not remove essential gear solely because the party might recover it.

Give rewards for resolving the problem. A negotiation that opens a route may fulfill the same contract as a fight. If rescuing a captive is the objective, payment should not secretly depend on defeating the captors afterward.

> Example: the crossing commission. A patron promises 80 coins to the company > for a rescue and safe access. Four heroes can divide that into 20 each. The rescued > workers also offer a Rope Coil and Lever and Wedges, each worth 5. If accepted, > those are two carried items, not 10 extra coins in addition to the items. The > party earns the contract payment whether it negotiates with the robbers or fights.

Selling and trading

Intact, useful gear sells for half its listed price, rounded down, or trades at full listed value with a willing trader. Pay a shortfall in coins. Unused trade value is not cash change, and a trade cannot be converted into coins or a cash-equivalent voucher at full value.

> Example: a recovered weapon. An ordinary melee weapon is worth 12 coins. > Selling it brings 6. A willing trader can instead accept it for 12 coins of goods: > a 5-coin rope, a 4-coin sleeping roll and a 3-coin water flask. The party cannot > trade it for a 12-coin credit note and immediately cash that note for 12 coins.

A market needs willing buyers as well as prices. Do not promise that a village will purchase unlimited identical goods. Equally, avoid inventing shortages only after a player has committed to a reasonable purchase. Establish unusual local conditions in advance and quote the offered price clearly.

Supplies with uncertain remaining quantities have no standard resale offer. A freshly acquired or crafted full supply can attract a half-price offer where there is demand. Special equipment needs an available buyer and an agreed valuation; apply the same half-sale/full-trade rule to that valuation. Gems and other treasure with a stated trade value do not suffer a second automatic halving.

Selling a card-granted item does not renew the grant. Learning an ability that uses a compatible item already owned does not create another copy to sell. The same ordinary weapon can serve several compatible attacks, with its Bulk counted once.

Supply is uncertain, not imaginary

After using an inventory supply, roll its die. On 1, step down: d20 → d12 → d10 → d8 → d6 → d4 → out. The use that empties it still works. The die tracks remaining supply without counting every arrow or mouthful.

A d4 healing bottle has a 25% chance to empty after each use. That does not mean it contains exactly four doses. A supply that has survived several checks remains at its current die until a check changes it.

The current market's healing bottles use d4: Lesser restores 6 HP, Greater 10, and Superior 16, before Life resistance and missing-HP limits. Their price buys potency as well as uncertain longevity. They do not require a healing spell roll or caster HP payment.

A potion still needs a free hand and the giver's Maneuver. A different recipient spends a Reaction unless at 0 HP. A bow, two-handed weapon, or weapon-and-shield combination occupies the hands that would otherwise use the bottle. Dropping an item is free; properly stowing it takes a Maneuver and can provoke. Apply those costs consistently to heroes and opponents.

Make special equipment personal

Ordinary weapons describe what the hero carries; their attack cards supply the mechanics. Special equipment adds the benefit actually printed on its card. A named sword does not acquire extra range or damage from its appearance alone.

An @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.077b2f43d810abd5.JournalEntryPage.7583def7f886433c]{Ember Edge} requires Flame 1 and adds 1 Fire damage to attacks made with that melee weapon, with Burning 1 on Strong. It does not turn a ranged attack into a compatible use. A hero may own it before meeting the requirement, but cannot use its special benefit until qualified.

A @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.dbe516a1a6e0520d.JournalEntryPage.48b5c622acdaf95f]{Cincture of Might} gives its printed Brawn benefit while worn. It does not stack with another positive Brawn item and does not recalculate creation DP or class eligibility. Use explicit card text for cursed items that suppress bonuses or set an attribute; a curse is not permission to invent a hidden exception after its bearer acts.

You can change an item's history and appearance to fit a campaign. A brass lens may come from a lighthouse or a buried observatory without changing its ability. Make mechanical changes explicit and review their effect on the party before introducing them as routine treasure.

Understanding what was found

An item states whether understanding is required to use it. Some magical weapons work at once; another object may require identification. Use the appropriate identification card and reveal what its outcome says. Possessing a mysterious object does not grant every fact about it, but ordinary inspection still reveals its visible form and obvious operation.

Give useful clues to dangerous properties. A written warning, an earlier owner's account or an observed effect lets the party investigate before committing. A curse can create a difficult decision without depending on the players having no chance to recognize risk.

Recipes, ingredients and work

Crafting requires an appropriate capability, a known recipe, its tools and actual ingredients. Cards that grant recipes provide those stated choices; additional recipes can come through Ordinary Recipe Study, discovery or derivation. They are not automatically available for coin purchase.

An identified object is not automatically a known recipe. Derivation uses its own ability, work intervals and cumulative target. Rare objects may require a long research project. Do not shorten that project through group rolls; neither crafting nor derivation uses group checks.

> Example: Bottled Morning. A crafter with this ability knows the Lesser Healing > Bottle recipe. With a mixing kit, moonmint, clean water and prepared life salts, > they spend one hour and roll Knowledge. The outcome raises one compatible supply > by 1/2/3 inventory steps, but the recipe's cap is d4. From out, any result therefore > produces a d4 bottle. Strong does not create three bottles or exceed the cap. > Check carried ingredients after the attempt. The recipe is not free stock.

The ordinary d6 material bundle costs 12 coins, while prepared healing ingredients cost 80 for their d6 bundle. Each bundle must contain the materials the recipe actually needs. Renaming common grass as life salts does not satisfy it. Foraging cards give practical ways to acquire suitable materials and deserve places where those materials can be found.

Services and lasting favors

A treatment appointment costs 10 coins for one eligible attempt; it does not promise complete recovery. Identification service likewise buys an attempt with the right capability, not a guaranteed Strong result. Daily limits still apply across different providers.

An ally might waive a fee, offer a workshop, or introduce a specialist as a reward. State the scope: one appointment, use of the bench for a week, or an introduction. This makes favors useful without turning every grateful person into a permanent source of unlimited labor. Hired people retain their own concerns and choices.
